notes: 20 more crops, each fully described: okra, bitter melon (goya), pumpkin (kabocha), watermelon, melon, peanut, burdock (gobo), ginger, shiso, basil, kale, beetroot, rocket, coriander, molokhia, water spinach, mitsuba, parsley, rakkyo and Swiss chard — with their sowing months for your climate, timings, feeding, care jobs and pests.
A new Herbs group when choosing your crops.
Behind the scenes: everything the app knows about each crop is now kept together in one place, and checked automatically, ready for many more crops. Nothing should look different.

A new garden starts with a few welcome steps: what the app does (and that your garden stays on your phone), restoring a backup, where your garden is, which crops you grow, your first bed or pot, and how to keep a backup. All can be skipped and changed later.

My crops (Tools): choose the crops you grow. They come first in every crop list (the rest are under “Other crops”), and the sowing calendar and crop ideas are about them. Until you choose, everything is shown as before.
Drop-down lists show headings where a list is grouped.

Timings follow your climate properly: packet days are for central Japan, so cooler places now take longer and warmer ones less (they came out the same everywhere before). Crops usually grown through winter, sown in spring where winters are hard (onions, peas in Hokkaido), take months, not most of a year.
Taro planted in April is ready in about 6 months (it showed almost a year): sprouting time now follows the soil warming over the following weeks, not just the planting day.
Sowing months are only offered where the crop can finish in time: no taro in Hokkaido, no mid-August corn in Tokyo.
Behind the scenes: every crop is now checked automatically, sown in every month it's offered, in four climates (Tokyo, Sapporo, Kagoshima, Naha), for timings that don't make sense.

A crop of your own now says which crop it's most like (tatsoi → komatsuna, okahijiki → spinach…). Everything you don't give — spacing, sowing months, growth, time to planting out, feeding, care jobs, pests, even its icon — comes from that crop, and what you give from the packet wins.
Crops of your own you added before show "not linked" in Products & seeds → Seeds & plants: edit one to choose what it's like.
Spray registrations don't carry over from the crop it's like: a spray registered for komatsuna isn't registered for tatsoi.
The test site can be installed as an app of its own, next to the real one (Chrome said it was already installed). The real app stays the same app on your phone.

Every crop has its own response to temperature — the cold below which it stops growing and the warmth at which it grows at full speed — instead of three groups. Eggplant, peppers and cucumbers now need more warmth than tomatoes and beans; celery and potatoes stop sooner in the cold than lettuce.

Crops of your own take their growing temperatures from the packet (生育適温, e.g. 15–25 °C) — when you add one, or with "edit this crop" in Products & seeds → Seeds & plants. Without them, their dates count plain days, and the crop says so.

Every crop has its own time to planting out and the sign it's ready — spinach about 3 weeks in mild weather, planted out young at 2–3 true leaves — instead of a stand-in figure for crops that didn't have one. Root crops, potatoes, taro, sweet potatoes and garlic say they aren't raised in trays.
The signs are in English ("at 4–5 true leaves").
For a crop of your own, starting seedlings asks for its days to planting out (from the packet); until then there's no plant-out date rather than a guess.
Crop ideas no longer suggest planting out heat-bolting crops (spinach, lettuce…) as the weather warms into summer.
Moving seedlings (indoors, under cover, outside): the card says where they are and since when — "outside since 23 Nov" — and editing asks the day you moved them.
The plant-out date counts the days they spent indoors as indoor days, instead of working it out as if they'd been in their new spot all along.

Seedlings that fill gaps now show in the planting's drawing, at their own (younger) size — move them to where they really are, and take out any that didn't make it, with Arrange plants by hand. A gap filled before this shows a "show it in the drawing" button.

Seedlings two (or more) to a pot or cell: say how many plants go in each new pot when you replant, and how many each holds when you start seedlings. Planting out a pot then plants all of its seedlings.

Replanting seedlings into a bed or bag where the same crop is already growing offers "fill gaps": they join that planting (replacing ones that didn't come up), instead of making a second planting of it. The planting shows when its gaps were filled.
Already planted some out as a separate planting next to the same crop? Its page offers to add them to the first one.
Placing seedlings by hand starts with the number you're planting out.
Seedlings you raised from seed are drawn by their real age (from sowing in the tray), so they no longer look bigger than older plants sown in the ground.

Seedlings: one Replant button instead of "Plant out" and "Pot on". Choose how many and when, then where: a bed, bag or pot in the garden, or another tray or pots to grow on. The rest stay where they are.

Your own tray and pot sizes, as many as you use: a 49-cell and a 9-cell tray side by side, 9 cm and 12 cm pots… Add or change them on the Seedlings page, or add a new size right where you choose the tray.
Planting seedlings out into a bed, bag or pot where something is already growing works: they go where you say. (Other new plantings ask once instead of refusing.)
A few seedlings into a bag or pot are drawn as that many plants.
Seedlings in trays and pots get the same looks as seeds in a bed: how many cells are up (or count them), again every few days until they're up — and planting out waits until they are.
Pot on: move some seedlings from a tray into 9 cm pots. They become their own group on the Seedlings page, to plant out later; the rest stay in the tray.
Plant out a few at a time into different beds, bags or pots — each lot becomes its own planting, and what's left stays in the tray. Discarding some keeps a note of why.
Crops sown in a continuous line are drawn as their sowing lines, widening as they grow, without a dot for every seed. Arranging plants by hand comes once they're thinned.

Crops sown in a continuous line (spinach, carrots, komatsuna…): when you look at how many have come up, count the seedlings along 10 cm of row instead of being told there are hundreds of "spots" — the app works out the share from how thickly it was sown.
A planting sown in a continuous line shows about how many plants it will be once thinned.

Checking that seeds have come up is now a few looks, not one answer: each time, say roughly how many are up (None yet, A few, A quarter… or a percentage, or count them), and when you looked. You can add a look from the planting's page too.

Nothing up yet? The app asks again in 3 days, and doesn't plan thinning until they're up — harvest is counted from when they do come up. Some crops (spinach especially) can take weeks in cold soil; re-sowing is only suggested once it's taking far longer than usual.

Some up? It asks again every few days until most are up or the number stops changing, then offers re-sowing the gaps. When they came up is worked out from your looks, and thinning and harvest follow it.
Your earlier answers are kept: a "Nothing came up" from the last few weeks becomes your first look, with the next one due now.

After answering a pop-up (like "Save the plan anyway?" or "Delete this planting?"), the app no longer sometimes jumps back to the page you were on — e.g. back to the planting form after the planting had already been saved, where saving again would make a second one.
Arranging plants by hand works again in beds with a net or other cover over them: taps go through the cover to the plants, and a tap close to a plant counts.

Products & seeds (Tools, the 📦 tile) has a tab for each kind of product, and a Seeds & plants tab for your varieties — each with its seed packet photos, used again whenever you plant that variety. Adding a variety of a crop the app doesn't know adds the crop too.
Watering jobs for everything you grow: each bed in the ground (watered much less often than pots — the soil holds far more), indoor pots and seedlings, as well as pots & bags.
Watering follows the latest forecast: it's fetched again whenever you open the app or come back to it, so a forecast that changes (say, rain that's no longer coming) changes the jobs too.

Care jobs follow growth, not the calendar: a cold spell pushes them back, and supports (nets, trellises, stakes) for crops that go through winter — like autumn-sown peas — go up in spring when they start climbing.
Seedlings: "Buy them" or "Sow from seed"; a planting that uses seedlings you started shows them instead.
Thinning advice is in English, and pre-filled for you to change.
The spray days page warns about bee-harmful ingredients in any product (neonicotinoids, pyrethroids, organophosphates and more), and lists which of your sprays have them.
Drop-down lists stay with their field when a pop-up scrolls.
Drop-down lists open right under the field again (crops, products and so on), instead of the phone's own picker or the bar above the keyboard.
Deleting something asks "are you sure?" again.
Both had stopped working in 1.26.0.

If your garden ever can't be loaded, a Recovery screen helps instead: keep a copy of what's stored, go back to one of this phone's daily copies, restore a backup file, or start again — nothing is saved over your garden while it can't be loaded.
Restoring a backup (file, daily copy or Google Drive) can be undone from Tools → Backup, and your photos are no longer cleared before a restore.
Backups made by older versions of the app are tested with every change, so they keep restoring correctly.
The app tells you when a newer version is out, with what's new, and shows what changed after it updates.
There's now a separate test site for trying out changes first, with its own data.
Very large beds no longer freeze the app; bed and pot sizes are checked as you type.
The garden map can zoom in when a big bed makes everything else tiny.
The ruler along beds no longer shows 0, never crowds, and round pots have none.
Behind the scenes: the app's code was reorganised so it's easier to keep working well. Nothing should look different.
